67) This does not mean that rationalism must deny the existence of objective reality.
It means that rationalism assumes our knowledge of reality does not depend on reality itself.
Rationalism can accept the usual definition of truth as an “adequation,” or correspondence, between reality and the discourse that reveals it.

But it will maintain that the truth of a discourse can be established independently of the reality that discourse expresses, and, so to speak, before that reality reveals itself in a non-discursive way through “sensory experience.”
The truth of discourse is determined by discourse itself—that is, by reason. Yet true discourse necessarily “corresponds” to the reality expressed by its meaning.
This is the conception of so-called ***a priori* truth**.
To explain how this is possible, rationalism generally maintains that reality has been “created,” or at least ordered, by some more or less divine reason.
Human reason proceeds on the assumption that a “divine” reason created actuality.
The discourses human reason finds within itself—true discourses, meaning those it can demonstrate to itself in a convincing way—must therefore “correspond” to the reality they concern.
Rationalism is consequently always more or less “idealist.”

68) It is true that omniscience must necessarily include the true claim that, first, reason cannot manifest itself—and therefore cannot exist—without reality, which exists independently of reason; and second, rational knowledge is impossible without sensory experience.
Yet, as “rationalism” maintains, the truth of this claim is established neither by reality itself nor even by experience. It is established by the complete discourse itself.
Only this form of rationalism is “realist” rather than “idealist,” and only it has no need of a “divine” reason.
To be true, the complete discourse must be not only articulated and meaningful but also coherent—that is, free of contradiction.
Yet precisely because it is complete, it must also contain mutually contradictory assertions.
To remain coherent, therefore, this discourse must be ⟨made up⟩ in such a way that when it contains two opposed assertions, one is judged true and the other false.
It must therefore contain not only every true discourse but also every partial and false discourse.
But it must include false discourses not as discourses mistakenly taken to be true, but precisely as false discourses.
Taken as a whole, the complete discourse can therefore be regarded as true.
In other words, the truth or falsity of its constituent parts is determined by the complete discourse itself, from within itself.
This agrees with the rationalist claim that reason is itself the criterion of the truth of the discourses it produces.

69) It must be said that, for rationalism in general—not only “naive” rationalism—the existence of many rational beings who nevertheless say different things is an extraordinarily awkward and frankly inexplicable fact.
Hegelianism, as we will see, does exactly the opposite: it explains why such contradictions within reason are necessary.

Chemistry is ultimately engaged in reducing an almost indefinite variety of chemical substances to just 92 “elements.”
The physicist then reduces these 92 “elements” still further, to two “elements”: combinations of electrons and protons.
Clearly, a result of this kind can be reached only through critical acts of identification.

77) Descartes clearly understood the failure of reflective rationalism. He saw that without a “divine guarantee” it remained entirely possible to doubt supposedly “self-evident” truths, including mathematical ones.
As a rule, this kind of rationalism therefore appeals, more or less openly, to the idea of a “divine” reason.
Reflective rationalism has to divide human reason in two.
First there is the reason that produces various coherent discourses. This is the reason presupposed by naive rationalism and rightly criticized by skepticism.

Then there is, so to speak, a higher reason—the Vernunft that German philosophy contrasts with Verstand. This higher reason reflects, hence my term “reflective rationalism,” on the discourses produced by the first reason and distinguishes those that are true, or evident, from those that are false or “doubtful.”
Every human being has his own “first” reason, since something that convinces me does not necessarily convince someone else.
But the higher reason is the same in everyone, since what is genuinely evident is evident to everyone.
It is therefore perfectly natural to regard this higher reason as standing above humanity—that is, as “divine,” eternal, and so on.
This divine reason possesses the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Human reason, by contrast, makes mistakes and knows truth only by participating in divine reason.
Divine reason creates reality. Human reason, by participating in divine reason, can therefore know reality before experience—that is, a priori.
Critical reason, incidentally, already operates with two forms of reason: one produces the various discourses, while the other identifies what they have in common.
In that case, however, the “divine” character of the second reason is less obvious.

78) This becomes especially clear in contemporary physics, above all in relativity theory, where only “invariant” qualities are treated as “real”—that is, qualities that remain unchanged when the coordinate system changes.
A change of coordinates mathematically represents the diversity of sensory experience:
“valid in this coordinate system” means, in effect, “this is how it appears to me”;
“valid in another system” means “this is how it appears to someone else.”
“Secondary” qualities are those that change when the coordinates change. “Primary” qualities are those that remain identical despite the change.
But the weakness of this method appears immediately.
Physics does not in fact use every possible change of coordinates. It uses only particular kinds of transformations.
The definition of which qualities count as “primary” is therefore arbitrary.

And if we decided that only qualities remaining unchanged under every conceivable transformation could count as primary, the result would not merely be an extraordinary impoverishment of reality. It would be its complete annihilation.

What distinguishes an apple from the “system of atoms” that constitutes it escapes physics.
But there is no reason to claim that whatever escapes physical knowledge must therefore escape knowledge altogether, still less that it does not exist.

And if one also assumes that this kind of irresponsible chatter is the basic meaning of human existence, then one must demand that the government above all refrain from interfering with it and never persecute anyone for their “personal convictions.” The skeptical origins of liberalism are particularly obvious in one of its fathers, Pierre Bayle. 86) Ancient philosophers lived in slave societies dominated by idle “masters.” They therefore naturally regarded work as an “inferior” activity and could not see it as part of the essence of human existence. As a result, they hardly moved beyond rationalist and empiricist interpretations.

Christianity, which addressed itself above all to people who labored like machines, gave human work a positive value. But the philosophical authority of the pagan thinkers was so great that throughout its Christian and bourgeois periods philosophy remained unable to overcome classical empiricism and rationalism.

Only when Hegel stripped Christian thought of its theological shell was the concept of work finally given a legitimate place in philosophy. Yet his bourgeois followers have still failed to grasp this. That is why the “experimentalism” or “technicalism” I will discuss later appears only among Hegel’s proletarian successors—that is, in Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.

Later, however, we will show in what sense contradictions—dialectical contradictions—can be attributed to reality itself.
